notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Prefill versus decode, and why input length drives time-to-first-token — NVIDIA: LLM inference sizing and performance

  • Prompt caching — reusing a prefix instead of re-prefilling it — Anthropic API: prompt caching

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • latency in agentic systems — where latency comes from in an agent.

  • Latency metrics — TTFT, inter-token latency, and how they're measured.

What this note adds: which term to attack first. The concept note establishes that latency is a sum over steps; this decomposes the sum, shows that prefill grows while decode doesn't, and gives the measurement that tells you whether you have a step problem, a context problem or a tool problem.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The sum? Σ over steps of (prefill + decode + tool time).
Which term grows? Prefill — input grows as context accumulates. Decode is per-step output.
First lever? Fewer steps. It divides every term at once.
What prefix caching fixes? The prefill term, and only if static content is first.
The measurement? Per-step TTFT, decode time, tool time — from your own traces.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

Agent latency is a sum over steps of prefill, decode and tool time, and the three behave differently. Decode is roughly constant per step because output length doesn't grow. Tool time is whatever your dependencies do. Prefill grows, because each step re-sends an accumulated context — so a late step in a long run is slower than an early one even doing identical work. That means the first lever is always fewer steps, since it divides every term at once, and the second is prefix caching, which attacks the growing term specifically.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Cut steps Always first. Steps multiply every other term. Scope, or moving work into deterministic code. Step count varies widely on similar inputs.
Parallelise tools Tool time dominates and calls are independent. Tokens for all branches; a race on shared writes. Several reads in sequence that needn't be.
Prefix caching Prefill dominates and the prefix is stable. Layout discipline — static content must come first. Late steps noticeably slower than early ones.
Smaller model per step Decode dominates on steps that don't need the frontier. Quality on those steps; a routing layer to maintain. Extraction and classification steps on the big model.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Cut steps Usually a workflow shape replacing part of the loop. Improves latency, cost and reliability together. Fewer spans per trace; failures name a function.
Parallel tools A fan-out and gather in the executor. Wall-clock down, tokens unchanged or up. Partial failure at the gather must be decided.
Prefix caching Prompt assembled static-first, mutable-tail only. Cuts prefill cost as well as time. Cache hit rate becomes a first-class metric.
Model routing A selection step plus per-tier evals. Cheaper per routed step. A quality delta per tier you must track.

The redraw test: parallelism and routing add boxes; caching adds a discipline about prompt order that doesn't show in a diagram at all — which is why it's the lever most often skipped.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

The decomposition. For a run of n steps:

latency ≈ Σ (prefill_i + decode_i + tool_i)

Decode is roughly flat per step. Tool time is your dependencies. Prefill scales with input length, and input length grows with accumulated context — so prefill_i rises with i even when the work is identical. That's why long runs feel like they slow down: they do.

Why fewer steps beats everything. Halving n halves the number of prefills, decodes and tool calls simultaneously — and because prefill grows with step index, removing late steps removes the most expensive ones. No other lever touches all three terms.

What caching actually buys. Prompt caching lets a stable prefix skip prefill on subsequent calls, which attacks precisely the growing term. The condition is an exact prefix match, so any mutation early in the prompt invalidates everything after it. Put system prompt and tool definitions first and confine all change to the tail, or the cache never hits and you've paid the complexity for nothing.

The measurement before any of this. Record TTFT, decode duration and tool duration per step. The three shapes tell you the answer: flat-and-many means a step problem, rising TTFT means a context problem, and a fat tool bar means the dependency is the problem and none of the model-side levers will help.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

flowchart TD
    A["⏱️ p95 too high"] --> B["📊 Break a trace into<br/>prefill / decode / tool per step"]
    B --> C{"🔀 Which dominates?"}
    C -->|"many steps"| D(["✂️ Cut steps — divides everything"])
    C -->|"tool time"| E{"🔀 Are the calls<br/>independent?"}
    C -->|"rising prefill"| F(["🗂️ Prefix caching + offload context"])
    C -->|"decode"| G(["🎚️ Smaller model on that step"])
    E -->|"yes"| H(["⚡ Parallelise"])
    E -->|"no"| I(["🔧 Fix the dependency, not the agent"])

    style A fill:#D1D5DB,stroke:#9CA3AF,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style B fill:#93C5FD,stroke:#60A5FA,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style C fill:#C4B5FD,stroke:#8B5CF6,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style E fill:#C4B5FD,stroke:#8B5CF6,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style D fill:#6EE7B7,stroke:#34D399,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style F fill:#6EE7B7,stroke:#34D399,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style G fill:#93C5FD,stroke:#60A5FA,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style H fill:#6EE7B7,stroke:#34D399,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style I fill:#FCD34D,stroke:#F59E0B,color:#000000,font-weight:bold

The first box is the one people skip. Optimising an agent's latency without the per-step breakdown is guessing, and the most common wrong guess is switching to a faster model when the time was in tool calls all along.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "We moved to a faster model and p95 barely moved."

Root cause. The team had assumed model inference dominated, because that's the visible part. The trace breakdown showed decode was about a fifth of the run — most of the time was tool calls made sequentially, several of which were independent lookups that could have run together, plus prefill that grew step over step because a large retrieved document sat in context from step two onward. The faster model improved the smallest term.

Fix. Parallelising the independent lookups and offloading the document to a reference took p95 down substantially, on the original model. The lesson is the ordering: measure the decomposition first, because three of the four levers are structural and only one is a model choice — and the model choice is the one that's easiest to reach for.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

Why does prefill grow when decode doesn't?

Because prefill processes the input and decode produces the output. Output length per step is roughly stable — a tool call or a paragraph — but input carries the accumulated trajectory, so it grows with every step that adds a result to context.

That asymmetry is why late steps are slower than early ones doing identical work, and why context management is a latency concern rather than only a cost one. The same offloading decision that reduces the token bill reduces time-to-first-token on every subsequent step.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Parallel tools is the biggest lever. Why isn't it always first?

Because it only helps if tool time actually dominates, and it costs tokens for every branch whether or not their results were needed. If the run is twelve steps of mostly model time, parallelising two tool calls changes little and adds a gather step to get wrong.

It's also constrained by correctness rather than by engineering — reads parallelise freely, writes to the same resource don't. So the honest sequence is: measure, cut steps, then parallelise the reads that remain. Leading with parallelism is optimising the term you haven't shown is the problem.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

At high concurrency, does the decomposition change?

Yes, and in a way that catches people. Under load your calls start queueing at the provider, so what shows up as increased TTFT isn't prefill growth at all — it's wait time before the request is served. The trace looks identical to a context problem and the fix is entirely different.

So at scale I'd separate queue wait from prefill in the instrumentation, because conflating them sends you optimising context when the answer is concurrency control or a higher rate limit. The second effect is that parallel tools multiply concurrent model calls, so the latency lever and the rate limit work against each other — parallelism that helps at low load can make p95 worse at high load by saturating your token budget.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design an agent to a 5-second p95 budget.

I'd allocate the budget before designing, because five seconds divides into very few steps. Assume roughly a second of tool time and a second of model time per step and you have room for two, maybe three — which immediately rules out an open loop and points at a planned shape: classify, retrieve in parallel, answer.

The structural choices follow from that allocation. A fixed graph rather than a free loop so step count can't vary, parallel retrieval so tool time is the max rather than the sum, prefix caching with a stable prefix so prefill stays flat, and a small model for the classification step so only the answer step pays frontier decode.

What I'd add for the tail is a deadline propagated into tool calls with a partial-answer path — at a hard p95 the right behaviour when a source is slow is to answer without it and say so, rather than to miss the budget. That's the §8 degradation ladder used as a latency control.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "A faster model is the latency fix."

✅ Reality: It attacks decode, which is often the smallest term. In most agent traces the time is in step count and tool calls. Measure the decomposition before choosing a lever, or you'll optimise the fifth of the run that was already fine.

❌ Trap: "Streaming makes it faster."

✅ Reality: Streaming changes perceived latency, not total. It's valuable and it's a different decision — total time to a complete answer is unchanged, and for anything feeding an automated consumer it buys nothing at all.

❌ Trap: "We enabled prompt caching but latency didn't improve."

✅ Reality: Caching needs an exact prefix match, so a rolling summary or a timestamp early in the prompt invalidates everything after it. Check the cache hit rate before concluding the feature doesn't work — the usual cause is prompt layout, not the cache.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • latency in agentic systems — the latency model.

  • caching in agentic systems — the caching tiers.

  • Latency metrics — TTFT and decode, defined.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §8 Fewer steps or more gates — the same first lever, from the reliability side.

  • §5 What gets cut when the window fills — offloading is a latency lever as well as a cost one.

  • §4 Parallel tool calls — the eligibility rule for the second lever.

  • §10 Caching tiers — prefix caching is where latency and cost optimisation coincide.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Voice / interview agent — the sub-second budget makes this the binding constraint.

  • §14 Deep research agent — parallel retrieval is the whole latency story.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Plan once and execute, versus deciding at every step — ReWOO: decoupling reasoning from observations (arXiv 2305.18323)

  • Prompt caching's prefix requirement, which is the constraint behind the cheapest lever — Anthropic API: prompt caching

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • latency in agentic systems — the latency model.

  • concurrency and parallelism — how parallel execution works.

What this note adds: the price list. Which term you attack finds the dominant term; this one says what each lever costs in something other than time — because every latency lever in an agent is paid for in tokens, quality, adaptivity or discipline, and a round that doesn't name the payment sounds like free lunch.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The only free lever? Prefix caching — costs layout discipline, nothing else.
What parallelism costs? Tokens for every branch, plus a race on shared writes.
What plan-once costs? Adaptivity — the plan can't react to what it finds.
What a smaller model costs? Quality on that step, and a routing layer to maintain.
What cutting steps costs? Scope, or work moved into deterministic code.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

Every latency lever in an agent is paid for in something, and naming the payment is what separates an answer from a wish. Prefix caching is the one near-free win — it costs prompt-layout discipline and nothing else, so it goes first. Parallel tools buy wall-clock with tokens. A smaller model per step buys time with quality on that step. Plan-once-then-execute buys predictability with adaptivity. Cutting steps is the biggest lever and it costs either scope or engineering, because the work moves into code. I'd apply them in that order — cheapest payment first.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Prefix caching Always — the prefix is stable across steps. Layout discipline: static first, mutation confined to the tail. Cache hit rate near zero while prefill dominates.
Parallel tools Tool time dominates and calls are independent reads. Tokens for every branch; correctness risk on shared writes. Sequential independent lookups.
Smaller model per step A step is extraction, classification or routing. Quality on that step; a routing layer and per-tier evals. Frontier model doing trivial work.
Plan once, then execute The steps are knowable and you need a predictable p95. Adaptivity — a wrong plan executes to the end. Step count varies but the work doesn't.
Cut steps Steps exist that code could own. Biggest lever. Scope, or engineering to move work into code. Steps that re-derive known things.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Prefix caching Prompt assembly becomes ordered and enforced. Cuts prefill cost and time — the only lever that helps both without a trade. Cache hit rate is a live metric; a layout regression shows there first.
Parallel tools Fan-out and gather; partial-failure policy at the gather. Wall-clock down, tokens flat or up, rate-limit pressure up. A gather that must decide what one dead branch means.
Smaller model A routing step and a model tier ladder. Cheaper and faster on routed steps. A quality delta per tier to track and re-check on upgrades.
Plan once A planner node feeding a bounded executor. Predictable p95; enables parallel execution of the plan. Re-plan rate is the signal that the planner is guessing.
Cut steps Deterministic code, often a workflow shape. Improves latency, cost and reliability at once. Fewer spans; failures name a function.

The redraw test: four of the five change the picture. Prefix caching doesn't — it's a rule about prompt order — which is exactly why it gets skipped despite being the cheapest thing on the list.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

Why caching is ordered first. It's the only lever whose payment isn't a trade-off — you give up the freedom to put mutable content early in the prompt, which you had no reason to want. Everything else on the list trades a property you might care about.

What parallelism actually buys. Wall-clock for k independent calls goes from Σ tᵢ to max tᵢ. Three calls at 800ms, 1.2s and 600ms: 2.6s sequential, 1.2s parallel. The payment is that all three run regardless of whether the second one's result made the third unnecessary — sequential execution can short-circuit and parallel cannot.

The plan-once trade, quantified. Deciding at each step means n model calls whose inputs grow; planning once means one larger call plus execution. The saving is n−1 prefills of an accumulating context, which is the fastest-growing term — and it's what lets the planned steps run in parallel, since they're all known up front. What you lose is the ability to change course on what step three returned.

The order, stated as a rule. Cheapest payment first: caching, then parallelism where reads allow, then model routing on steps that don't need the frontier, then plan-once if the shape permits, then cutting steps — which is the biggest win and the biggest commitment.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

flowchart TD
    A["⏱️ Need to save time"] --> B{"🔀 Is prefix caching<br/>hitting?"}
    B -->|"no"| C(["🗂️ Fix prompt layout first — free"])
    B -->|"yes"| D{"🔀 Independent reads<br/>run sequentially?"}
    D -->|"yes"| E(["⚡ Parallelise — pay in tokens"])
    D -->|"no"| F{"🔀 Frontier model on<br/>a trivial step?"}
    F -->|"yes"| G(["🎚️ Route down — pay in quality there"])
    F -->|"no"| H{"🔀 Are the steps<br/>knowable up front?"}
    H -->|"yes"| I(["🗺️ Plan once — pay in adaptivity"])
    H -->|"no"| J(["✂️ Cut steps — pay in scope"])

    style A fill:#D1D5DB,stroke:#9CA3AF,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style B fill:#C4B5FD,stroke:#8B5CF6,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style D fill:#C4B5FD,stroke:#8B5CF6,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style F fill:#C4B5FD,stroke:#8B5CF6,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style H fill:#C4B5FD,stroke:#8B5CF6,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style C fill:#6EE7B7,stroke:#34D399,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style E fill:#93C5FD,stroke:#60A5FA,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style G fill:#93C5FD,stroke:#60A5FA,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style I fill:#FCD34D,stroke:#F59E0B,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style J fill:#FCD34D,stroke:#F59E0B,color:#000000,font-weight:bold

Walking it in order matters because the payments escalate. By the time you reach the bottom two you're giving up capability, and it's worth having exhausted the ones that don't first — most teams arrive at "use a smaller model" without ever checking their cache hit rate.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "We parallelised everything and p95 got worse under load."

Root cause. The team fanned out every independent call, which helped in staging where they were the only traffic. In production each run now issued four or five concurrent model and tool calls, so tokens-per-minute against the provider scaled with concurrency times fan-out. They hit the account rate limit at a fraction of expected traffic, requests started returning 429s, the harness retried, and retries consumed more of the same budget — so the parallelism that saved time at low load was queueing at high load while still costing tokens for every branch.

Fix. Parallelism was capped per run rather than being unbounded fan-out, and a global concurrency lease was introduced so total in-flight calls stayed under the provider budget. The general point: parallelism's payment is tokens and rate-limit headroom, and the second one only presents itself at scale — which is why the lever that tests best in staging is the one most likely to surprise you.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

You call prefix caching free. Nothing's free — what's the catch?

The catch is a constraint rather than a cost: the prefix has to be byte-identical across calls, so anything mutable must sit after everything static. In practice that means the system prompt and tool definitions first, and the rolling summary, retrieved content and conversation tail after them.

That's a discipline, not a trade — you weren't gaining anything by putting a timestamp early in the prompt. It's free in the sense that no capability is surrendered, which is not true of any other lever here.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Plan-once saves prefills but loses adaptivity. How do you decide?

By checking whether the adaptivity is actually used. I'd sample traces and count how often a step's arguments genuinely depended on a previous step's result, rather than merely following it. If that fraction is low, I'm paying accumulating prefill for a capability the workload doesn't exercise.

Where it's high — investigation, debugging, search — planning once produces a plan that's wrong by step three, and the hybrid is better: plan once, execute, and allow a bounded number of re-plans. That keeps most of the predictability while retaining a way to recover.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

Which of these levers behaves differently at 100× traffic?

Parallelism, badly — as in the failure story. It's the lever whose payment includes a shared resource, so its cost is superlinear in concurrency while its benefit is flat. Everything else scales neutrally: caching gets better with volume if the prefix is shared, routing and step-cutting are per-run properties.

The subtler one is caching. A shared prefix across many runs means high hit rates, but cache entries have a lifetime, so low-traffic tenants may never hit a warm cache while high-traffic ones always do. That produces a latency difference between customers that has nothing to do with their workload, and it's worth knowing about before someone reports it as a bug.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

The product wants both lower p95 and lower cost. Which levers serve both?

Two do. Cutting steps improves latency, cost and reliability together, which is why it's always worth doing first even though it's the hardest. Prefix caching cuts prefill time and the tokens billed for that prefill, so it also serves both.

Model routing serves both but pays in quality on the routed steps, so it needs per-tier evals before you can claim it's free. Parallelism serves only latency and actively worsens cost — it's the lever to reach for when latency is the binding constraint and the budget has room.

So the honest answer to "both" is: cut steps, fix caching, route where quality allows, and don't parallelise until you've established that latency matters more than the token line. Presenting it as an ordering rather than a menu is what makes it a design answer rather than a list.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "Parallelise everything — it's the biggest latency lever."

✅ Reality: It's the biggest lever on tool time specifically, and it pays in tokens and rate-limit headroom. Unbounded fan-out that wins in staging loses at scale when concurrent calls saturate your provider budget.

❌ Trap: "Use a smaller model — it's faster and cheaper, so it's strictly better."

✅ Reality: It's faster and cheaper on that step and worse at it. That's fine for extraction and classification and not fine for planning. Route by step, evaluate each tier, and know your quality delta before you rely on it.

❌ Trap: "We've optimised latency — we switched models and added streaming."

✅ Reality: Streaming changes perception, not duration, and a model swap attacks decode, which is often the smallest term. Neither touches step count or prefill growth, which is where agent latency usually lives.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • latency in agentic systems — the model this prices.

  • caching in agentic systems — the caching tiers.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §9 Which term you attack — this note is what you do once that says where.

  • §4 Parallel tool calls — the eligibility rule behind the second lever.

  • §10 Model routing and caching tiers — two of these levers are cost decisions as well.

  • §3 ReAct vs plan-and-execute — plan-once seen from the latency side.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Voice / interview agent — a sub-second budget forces most of this list at once.

  • §14 Support agent that takes actions — routing down the classification step is the usual first win.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Streaming events — token deltas alongside tool-use and lifecycle events — Anthropic API: streaming messages

  • Streaming agent output, including intermediate steps — LangGraph: streaming

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • Streaming Agent Output — how streaming is implemented.

  • streaming and real-time agents — streaming in production agents.

What this note adds: that streaming is a product commitment, not a transport setting. Deciding to stream progress means deciding what the user is allowed to see — including work you may later discard — and that's a decision about honesty as much as about latency.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Four things you can stream? Tokens · tool-call events · status/progress · partial results.
Which matters most for agents? Progress. A silent 30s gap is where users abandon.
What streaming doesn't change? Total latency. Only perception.
The commitment? Anything shown may be wrong or later discarded — say so.
Who gains nothing? An automated consumer. It waits for the whole thing regardless.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

Streaming tokens is the default people think of, but for an agent the valuable thing is streaming progress — which tool is running, what step it's on, what it has found so far. An agent spends most of a long run not producing tokens, so token streaming leaves the same silent gaps that make users abandon. The commitment worth naming is that anything I show may later be discarded or corrected: a retrieved source that turns out irrelevant, a plan that changes. Streaming progress means designing for visible revision rather than presenting intermediate state as fact.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Nothing — return the result Automated consumers, batch, or sub-second runs. Silent waiting; users abandon on long runs. No human watching.
Token streaming only A single long generation at the end. Still silent during tool calls, which is most of an agent run. One big answer, few tools.
Progress events Multi-step runs a human is waiting on. The default. An event schema to design and a UI to consume it. Runs over a few seconds with tool calls.
Progress + partial results Results accumulate and early ones are useful. Users see work that may later be revised or dropped. Research, multi-source gathering.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Nothing Request/response. Simplest. Abandonment is invisible — you can't tell a slow run from a lost user.
Tokens A streaming transport and a client that assembles. No change. Reconnection and resume-from-offset become client concerns.
Progress events An event schema: step started, tool called, status. Emitted from the loop. Negligible payload. The schema is a contract — changing it breaks clients.
Partial results Results streamed as produced, with revision semantics. Same tokens. You must handle retraction: what happens when a shown finding is dropped.

The redraw test: progress streaming means the loop emits events outward at every step, so the diagram gains an event channel alongside the response. If the only arrow out is the final answer, the run is silent by construction.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

Why token streaming isn't enough for agents. In a chat completion the model is generating almost the whole time, so token streaming fills the wait. In an agent run the model generates in short bursts between tool calls — so most of the elapsed time produces no tokens at all. A run that takes thirty seconds with three seconds of generation is twenty-seven seconds of silence under token-only streaming.

Perceived versus total. Streaming does not reduce total latency by a millisecond. What it changes is the wait shape: time-to-first-signal drops from the full run to the first event. That's a real product improvement and it's worth being precise that it's a different metric — a round that claims streaming improved p95 is making an error someone will catch.

The revision rate you should know. If you stream partial results, measure how often a shown result is later dropped or corrected. A low rate means partials are safe to present plainly; a high rate means they need framing as provisional, or shouldn't be shown at all. Streaming findings that are frequently retracted trains users to distrust the whole output.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

flowchart TD
    A["🏃 A run starts"] --> B{"🔀 Is a human<br/>waiting?"}
    B -->|"no"| C(["📦 Return the result — streaming buys nothing"])
    B -->|"yes"| D{"🔀 Will it be silent<br/>for more than a few seconds?"}
    D -->|"no"| E(["🔤 Token streaming is enough"])
    D -->|"yes"| F(["📡 Emit progress events per step"])
    F --> G{"🔀 Are intermediate results<br/>useful on their own?"}
    G -->|"yes"| H(["📄 Stream partials — with revision semantics"])
    G -->|"no"| I(["🔄 Status only — tool name and step"])

    style A fill:#D1D5DB,stroke:#9CA3AF,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style B fill:#C4B5FD,stroke:#8B5CF6,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style D fill:#C4B5FD,stroke:#8B5CF6,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style G fill:#C4B5FD,stroke:#8B5CF6,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style C fill:#6EE7B7,stroke:#34D399,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style E fill:#6EE7B7,stroke:#34D399,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style F fill:#93C5FD,stroke:#60A5FA,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style H fill:#FCD34D,stroke:#F59E0B,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style I fill:#6EE7B7,stroke:#34D399,color:#000000,font-weight:bold

The last branch is the one with product consequences. Status events are safe — "searching the knowledge base" can't be wrong in a way that matters. Partial results can be, so streaming them is a commitment to showing your working, revisions included.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "Users kept stopping the agent mid-run and complaining it was broken."

Root cause. The agent streamed tokens, which the team considered solved. But a typical run spent twenty-odd seconds in retrieval and tool calls before generating anything, so the user saw nothing at all for most of the wait — and a blank screen after clicking is indistinguishable from a hang. They cancelled, retried, and cancelled again, which also meant the expensive early steps were repeatedly paid for and discarded.

Fix. Progress events from the loop — step started, tool name, a human-readable status — rendered as a live activity list. Total latency didn't change at all; abandonment dropped sharply. The framing worth keeping is that the problem was never latency, it was uncertainty, and those need different fixes.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

Streaming progress means exposing internals. Is that a good idea?

Selectively. I'd expose what the user can act on or reason about — which source is being checked, which step it's on — and not raw model reasoning or internal tool arguments, which are noise at best and leak implementation at worst.

The framing I'd use is that the event stream is a product surface with its own design, not a debug log turned on in production. It has a schema, it's versioned, and what goes in it is a deliberate choice rather than everything the loop happens to know.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Streaming partial results risks showing something you later retract. Why do it?

Because for some tasks the partials are the value. In research, seeing sources appear as they're found lets the user redirect early — they can tell at source three that the agent is off track, which saves the rest of the run.

The trade is that you're committing to revision semantics: a way to mark a result as superseded, and a UI that handles it. If the answer is "we'd just remove it silently", I'd rather not stream partials at all, because silent disappearance is worse than never having shown it.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

What breaks about streaming at scale or over bad networks?

Connection lifetime, mostly. A streamed response holds a connection for the run's duration, so at scale you're bounded by concurrent connections rather than by compute, and intermediaries — load balancers, proxies — will idle-timeout a stream that goes quiet during a long tool call. That's an argument for heartbeat events regardless of whether you have progress to report.

Reconnection is the other half. A client that drops mid-run needs to resume without replaying everything or losing the run, which means events need sequence numbers and the server needs a short buffer. That's the point where streaming stops being a transport flag and becomes a small piece of distributed-systems design — and it's why the async job-id shape from §2 is often the better answer for genuinely long runs, with the stream as a view onto it rather than the run's only handle.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design the event stream for an agent platform many teams build clients against.

I'd define a small closed event vocabulary — run started, step started, tool called, tool returned, partial result, result revised, run finished, run failed — with a stable schema and a sequence number on every event. Closed matters: if teams can emit arbitrary event types, clients can't be written once, and the stream becomes unversioned.

Content is where I'd give teams control but with constraints. Each event carries a machine field and a human-readable label the team supplies, so a client can render progress without understanding any particular agent's domain. That way a generic UI works for every agent, which is the thing a platform is for.

Separately I'd keep the stream distinct from the trace. They look similar and serve different masters — the trace is complete, internal and retained for debugging; the stream is curated, external and ephemeral. Teams that emit one from the other end up either leaking internals to users or losing detail they needed at 3am.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "We stream, so latency is handled."

✅ Reality: Streaming changes perceived wait, not duration. The run takes exactly as long. It's a genuine improvement and it belongs in a different row of the table from the levers that actually reduce time.

❌ Trap: "Token streaming is streaming."

✅ Reality: For an agent most elapsed time produces no tokens — it's tool calls. Token-only streaming leaves the long silences intact, which is exactly where users abandon. Progress events are the agent-relevant form.

❌ Trap: "Stream everything the loop knows — more transparency is better."

✅ Reality: The stream is a product surface, not a debug log. Raw reasoning and tool arguments confuse users and leak implementation detail. Curate the vocabulary and keep the full record in the trace.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • Streaming Agent Output — the implementation.

  • streaming and real-time agents — streaming in production.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §9 Transport — what you stream decides what transport you need.

  • §2 Sync vs async runs — a held stream is the sync side; long runs want a job id plus a stream view.

  • §12 Tracing — the trace and the stream are different artifacts and shouldn't be one.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Deep research agent — streaming found sources is the product, not a nicety.

  • §14 Voice / interview agent — streaming is the interaction rather than a progress indicator.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Voice-mode latency budgets and the turn-taking loop — OpenAI: Realtime API

  • Endpointing and barge-in in a streaming speech pipeline — Deepgram: streaming speech-to-text

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • voice agents — the voice agent architecture end to end.

  • streaming and real-time agents — real-time agents generally.

What this note adds: the budget allocation. A sub-second turn has to be divided across endpointing, STT, the model and TTS, and once it's divided almost every other decision in this vault is forced — which is why voice is the case where latency stops being an optimisation and becomes the architecture.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The chain? Endpointing → STT → LLM → TTS → playback.
What usually dominates? Endpointing — waiting to be sure the user stopped.
How many tool calls fit? Roughly zero to one. Multi-step loops don't fit a turn.
What barge-in must reach? TTS playback and in-flight tool calls, not just the loop.
The cheat that buys most? Start TTS on the first sentence, not the full response.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

A conversational turn budget is a few hundred milliseconds of perceived gap, and it has to cover endpointing, transcription, the model and speech synthesis. That division forces everything else: there's room for about one tool call, so a multi-step agent loop cannot run inside a turn — anything longer has to be acknowledged verbally and continued behind a filler utterance. The two techniques that buy the most are streaming TTS from the first sentence rather than the complete response, and aggressive endpointing tuned against false cut-offs.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Everything in the turn Simple Q&A with no tools or one fast lookup. Any slow tool blows the budget audibly. Answers come from the model or one cache.
Filler then continue A tool call may exceed the budget. The agent says something while working — must sound natural. "Let me check that for you."
Speech-to-speech model Latency is paramount and the task fits one model. Less control over the pipeline; fewer tool options. Conversational, low tool use.
Async for the slow path The request genuinely needs a long agent run. Breaks the conversational frame — becomes "I'll get back to you". Research-grade questions asked by voice.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
In-turn A tight STT→LLM→TTS chain, streaming at every hop. No room for retries — a retry is an audible pause. p95 per stage, not per run. The tail is what users hear.
Filler + continue A filler generator and a resume-speaking path. One extra short generation per slow turn. Filler-rate is a UX metric: too many and it sounds evasive.
Speech-to-speech One model replaces three stages. Usually cheaper in latency, different in cost. Less observability — fewer seams to instrument.
Async A job plus a callback; the conversation continues meanwhile. Normal agent economics. You now have two interaction modes to keep coherent.

The redraw test: a voice agent's diagram is a pipeline with a budget annotated on every hop. If the boxes have no milliseconds on them, the design hasn't been done — a voice architecture is its latency allocation.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "It interrupts people mid-sentence, and when you interrupt it, it keeps talking."

Root cause. Two ends of the same defect. Endpointing was tuned aggressively to protect the turn budget, so a natural pause mid-sentence was read as end-of-turn and the agent started answering a half-finished question. In the other direction, barge-in cancelled the LLM generation but not the TTS playback already buffered on the client, nor the tool call that generation had triggered — so the agent talked over the user and then acted on a request they had abandoned.

Fix. Endpointing gained a short adaptive hold informed by prosody rather than silence alone, and barge-in became a cancellation that propagated to playback, generation and in-flight tools — the §7 cancellation problem with a sub-second deadline. The general lesson: in voice, cancellation has to reach every stage of the pipeline, and a cancel that stops one stage is worse than none because the user believes they stopped it.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • voice agents — the architecture in full.

  • streaming and real-time agents — streaming foundations.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §7 Cancellation & timeouts — barge-in is that decision at a sub-second deadline.

  • §9 Transport — a voice turn is what forces WebRTC over WebSocket.

  • §9 What each second costs — the budget makes most levers mandatory rather than optional.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Voice / interview agent — this note is that problem's core constraint.

  • §14 Support agent that takes actions — voice front-ends inherit the whole budget.

📚 Reference Links

  • Server-sent events — one-way, over plain HTTP, with built-in reconnection — MDN: Server-sent events

  • WebRTC for real-time audio, and why it beats WebSocket there — WebRTC: getting started

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • choosing-realtime-transport — the general transport decision.

  • webrtc-vs-websocket-for-audio — the audio-specific comparison.

What this note adds: the agent-specific mapping. The networking notes own the transports; this says which agent shape wants which — and that the answer is SSE far more often than teams assume, because agent output is one-directional.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Default for agent streams? SSE — output is one-way, and it reconnects for free.
When WebSocket? Genuine bidirectional need mid-run: interrupts, live input.
When WebRTC? Audio. Anything else is over-engineering.
The proxy hazard? Buffering and idle timeouts kill a quiet stream.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

Agent output is one-directional — the run emits events and the client consumes them — so SSE is the right default and it's underused. It's plain HTTP, it carries auth and infrastructure unchanged, and reconnection with a last-event id is part of the spec rather than something you build. I move to WebSocket only when the client genuinely needs to send mid-run: interrupts, live corrections, collaborative input. WebRTC is for audio, where jitter buffers and loss handling matter, and using it for text events is complexity nobody needs.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
SSE One-way event stream to a browser or service. The default. No client-to-server channel on the same connection. Progress events, token deltas, status.
WebSocket Mid-run bidirectional traffic. Your own reconnection, heartbeat and framing logic. Interrupts, live user input during a run.
WebRTC Real-time audio or video. Signalling, ICE, TURN — a real infrastructure commitment. Voice agents with sub-second turns.
Polling a job Long runs, backend callers, no live UI. Latency between polls; no push. Server-to-server, minutes-long runs.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
SSE A streaming endpoint; normal HTTP infrastructure. Connection held for the run. Proxy buffering and idle timeouts are the failure mode — heartbeats fix both.
WebSocket A connection manager, heartbeats, reconnect logic. Same connection cost, more code. Sticky sessions or shared state if the run outlives one node.
WebRTC Signalling server, STUN/TURN, media pipeline. TURN relay bandwidth is a real cost line. An infrastructure surface of its own.
Polling A status endpoint and a job store. Poll traffic. Simplest to operate; the async shape from §2.

The redraw test: transport choice changes the edge of the diagram, not the agent. If picking one changes anything inside the loop, something is coupled that shouldn't be.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "Streams die after about a minute in production and work perfectly locally."

Root cause. SSE over a load balancer with a 60-second idle timeout. The agent's stream was genuinely idle during long tool calls — no events to send — so the connection looked dead to the proxy and was closed. Locally there was no proxy, so it never reproduced. The client's automatic reconnect then re-established a stream that produced nothing for another minute and died again, which looked like the agent hanging rather than like a transport problem.

Fix. Periodic heartbeat comments on the stream so it's never idle from the proxy's perspective, plus a last-event id so a genuine reconnect resumes rather than restarting. The general shape — an idle timeout somewhere in the path you don't control — is the most common streaming failure and it applies equally to WebSocket.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • choosing-realtime-transport — the general decision.

  • server-sent-events — SSE mechanics including reconnection.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §9 Stream progress — what you stream decides what the transport must carry.

  • §2 Sync vs async runs — polling is the async side; streams are the held-connection side.

  • §9 Voice turn budget — audio is what forces WebRTC.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Voice / interview agent — WebRTC and its TURN costs.

  • §14 Deep research agent — SSE with heartbeats for a minutes-long run.
